description:
On Lytton Road in Old Anarkali, directly opposite the Anarkali station of the Orange Line Metro Train, stands the Jain Mandir, one of the last physical reminders of Lahore's once-substantial Jain community. Built around 1940 to serve the city's Bhabra Jain merchant families — Punjab having historically been home to a significant Jain trading population — the temple follows a shikhara-style form typical of North Indian Jain architecture and was dedicated to the veneration of the Tirthankaras, the enlightened teacher-figures central to Jain belief and practice. Like much of Lahore's pre-Partition religious minority heritage, the temple fell into disuse after 1947, when the great majority of the city's Jain and Hindu population departed for India. Its most severe blow came in 1992, when it was heavily vandalised in retaliation for the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, India, leaving the building damaged and effectively abandoned for three decades. The turning point came in December 2021, when Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered its restoration, leading to an eight-month conservation effort. The temple reopened in June 2022, allowing religious use to resume after a hiatus of roughly thirty years — an unusual and widely reported instance in Pakistan of an active return to worship, rather than mere heritage preservation, at a minority religious site. Though Jainism has only a residual presence in contemporary Pakistan, the temple's revival has been framed in Pakistani and international press as a significant, if modest, gesture of religious pluralism, and the building today stands as a rare functioning Jain place of worship anywhere in the country, embedded within the dense, historically layered streetscape of Old Anarkali. Independent, established-press reporting adds further precision to this account: Dawn's Sheharyar Rizwan reports that the temple was "constructed by a woman with her own resources in 1940," though her name is not recorded in the surviving coverage, and that after the 1992 attack "the temple's canopy was the only piece of the original structure that survived"; its ruins then lay neglected for over two decades until, in 2016, the remaining site was enclosed behind a boundary wall and the land given away to the Orange Line Metro Train project. The Supreme Court's restoration order, issued in December 2021 by then Chief Justice Gulzar Ahmed, came a day before the nineteenth anniversary of the Babri Masjid's demolition and was reported by the Express Tribune to run alongside a parallel restoration case for Lahore's Neela Gumbad (Blue Tomb); of at least a dozen Jain temples once standing in the city, per Youlin Magazine, this is the sole survivor, and it is not listed among the Punjab Archaeology Department's own "Religious Monuments."

## Bibliography
- Sheharyar Rizwan, "Under-reconstruction Jain Mandir in Lahore all set to reopen," *Dawn*, 1 April 2022.
- "Pakistan set to reopen Lahore's famous Jain temple," *The Express Tribune*, 5 December 2021.
- Muhammad Asif Nawaz, "Story of the Jain Mandir," *Youlin Magazine*, 20 July 2022.
qa_note: Sources disagree slightly on the exact construction period: Dawn (1 April 2022) states the temple was built specifically "in 1940," while Youlin Magazine (20 July 2022) hedges that "it is safe to assume it came about in late 1930s or early 1940s"; neither source names the woman credited with funding its construction, and this is reported rather than resolved. Separately, Dawn's April 2022 report quotes ETPB's Faraz Abbas estimating restoration completion "in just over a month" (around May 2022) with "over 70pc" of work then done; no source verified in this research pass confirms whether that timeline held, so the June 2022 reopening date given elsewhere in this entry is not independently reconfirmed here.
